report:
**Conclusion: The claim is false.** There is no credible scientific evidence that drinking boiled garlic water cures or prevents COVID-19.

**Evidence behind this conclusion:**

The World Health Organization directly addressed this claim in its official COVID-19 Mythbusters resource, stating that while garlic has some antimicrobial properties, "there is no evidence from the current outbreak that eating garlic has protected people from the new coronavirus" (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters). This assessment was echoed by health authorities cited in ITV News, which reported the WHO's warning that garlic, along with chlorine sprays and hot baths, does not prevent coronavirus infection (https://www.itv.com/news/2020-03-10/garlic-spraying-yourself-with-chlorine-and-hot-baths-do-not-prevent-coronavirus-world-health-organisation-warns).

Independent fact-checking organizations reached the same conclusion. AFP Fact Check noted that health professionals debunked garlic-based COVID "cures" as early as February 2020, at the very start of the pandemic, finding no evidence supporting their use as effective treatment (https://factcheck.afp.com/theres-no-scientific-proof-tonic-onions-ginger-garlic-and-lemon-can-cure-covid-19). Similarly, Rappler's fact-check confirmed there is no official cure or preventive treatment for COVID-19, explicitly rating claims about garlic, ginger, and heat as false, noting these have been debunked by both the WHO and fact-checkers worldwide (https://www.rappler.com/newsbreak/fact-check/264621-heat-garlic-ginger-cure-covid-19/).

**Bottom line:** Garlic may have general antimicrobial properties in laboratory settings, but no clinical evidence supports it as a treatment or cure for COVID-19 in humans. This claim originated and spread widely early in the pandemic and has been consistently debunked by the WHO and multiple independent fact-checkers.
